title: Information Technology Act s. 66E — Statutory provision (Information Technology Act s. 66E)

content.overview: Violation of privacy under Information Technology Act, 2000 — section 66E. Section 66E concerns intentionally or knowingly capturing, publishing or transmitting the image of a private area of any person without consent, in circumstances violating privacy, subject to the statutory conditions. The analysis must identify each statutory ingredient, the required mental element, the computer-resource/device nexus, the evidence supporting attribution, applicable jurisdiction and the precise criminal consequence.

content.study:
Statutory rule
Section 66E concerns intentionally or knowingly capturing, publishing or transmitting the image of a private area of any person without consent, in circumstances violating privacy, subject to the statutory conditions.

Ingredient-by-ingredient analysis
Identify the actus reus, the required knowledge/intent or other mental element, the relevant computer resource/communication device or digital act, and the facts proving each element. Do not infer criminal liability merely from ownership, possession, account access or use of a device.

Evidence and procedure
Separate admissibility from proof. Electronic records should be analysed under BSA 2023 s. 63 where applicable, with authenticity, integrity, source and chain of custody addressed separately. Identify the investigating authority, territorial/cross-border facts, limitation and competent criminal forum.

Boundary with neighbouring provisions
Do not substitute section 66E with sections 43/43A or other offence provisions merely because the same incident involves unauthorised access, loss or data. Identify cumulative offences only where their independent ingredients are proved.

Current-law caution
Section 66A is struck down and must not be pleaded as a current offence. State the exact statutory provision actually engaged.

sections.body: Test consent, knowledge, intent, attribution, authority, statutory exceptions and evidentiary gaps. State the precise relief, charge or defence consequence rather than a generic cyber-law conclusion.

cases.name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
cases.facts: The Court reviewed restrictions on online speech under the Information Technology Act.
cases.issue: Whether IT Act s. 66A impermissibly restricted constitutional speech.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Section 66A was vague and overbroad and violated Article 19(1)(a); it was not saved by Article 19(2).
cases.holding: Section 66A was struck down in its entirety.
cases.relevance: Use only as historical status; do not present s. 66A as a current offence.

cases.name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
cases.facts: The Court examined the statutory method for proving electronic records.
cases.issue: Whether electronic records can be admitted without the applicable certificate route.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Electronic records must satisfy the special statutory proof requirements applicable to computer outputs.
cases.holding: The Court reaffirmed the certificate discipline for electronic evidence.
cases.relevance: Use with BSA s. 63 and digital-record admissibility.

cases.name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
cases.facts: The Constitution Bench considered privacy as a constitutional right in the digital and modern State.
cases.issue: Whether privacy is protected as a Fundamental Right.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Privacy is intrinsic to dignity, liberty and Part III, subject to legality, legitimate aim, proportionality and procedural safeguards.
cases.relevance: Use for surveillance, data protection and informational privacy.

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE AND JURISDICTION
Whether Information Technology Act s. 66E — Statutory provision (Information Technology Act s. 66E) applies to the stated facts and whether the chosen forum and remedy are maintainable.

II. GOVERNING RULE
Information Technology Act s. 66E — Statutory provision (Information Technology Act s. 66E) is governed by Information Technology Act, 2000, allied rules, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 where applicable, BSA 2023 and constitutional privacy principles. identify the date, technology, applicable IT Act provision, data regime, intermediary rule and evidence law; distinguish struck-down provisions from current offences.

III. INGREDIENT APPLICATION
Identify each condition, connect it to the evidence and answer the principal exception or defence. Apply BSA s. 63 to digital records where relevant and state the initial burden precisely.

IV. CONCLUSION
Grant, refuse or modify the relief only to the extent authorised by the governing law and proved record.

I. STATEMENT OF FACTS AND PROCEDURAL PROVENANCE
Set out the material facts, forum, procedural stage, notices, pleadings and documents.

II. STATUTORY AND DOCTRINAL SCHEME
Deconstruct Information Technology Act s. 66E — Statutory provision (Information Technology Act s. 66E) under Information Technology Act, 2000, allied rules, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 where applicable, BSA 2023 and constitutional privacy principles, including its purpose, conditions, exceptions and connected provisions.

III. SATISFACTION OF MANDATORY INGREDIENTS
Apply each ingredient to the record, address jurisdiction, limitation, maintainability and the opposing party's strongest objection.

IV. VERIFIED AUTHORITIES
Use the case ratios below only for the propositions they decide and distinguish contrary facts.

V. EVIDENCE AND PRAYER
Address BSA ss. 63, 104 and 109 where relevant, then seek the precise order available from the designated cyber-crime police and criminal court, adjudicating officer, civil court, High Court under Articles 226/227, or competent data-protection and regulatory forum.
